title.sl: Želje in všečnost: want to, would like to, enjoy -ing
title.de: Wünsche und Vorlieben: want to, would like to, enjoy -ing
title.it: Desideri e gusti: want to, would like to, enjoy -ing
title.en: Wishes and likes: want to, would like to, enjoy -ing

rule.sl:
**want to** + osnovna oblika pove naravnost, kaj hočeš: **I want to go home.** (Hočem domov.) **Jack wants to buy a dog.** (Jack hoče kupiti psa.) V govoru slišiš **wanna**.

**would like** (kratko **'d like**) pove isto vljudno, za vse enako. S stvarjo: **I'd like a cup of tea.** (Prosim skodelico čaja.) Z glagolom **to** + osnovna oblika: **I'd like to stay.** (ne *I'd like stay*). Ponudba: **Would you like a scone?** (Bi scone?) **Yes, please.** (Ja, prosim.) **No, thank you.** (Ne, hvala.) **I'd love to.** (Z veseljem.)

Vljudna prošnja: **Could you pass the salt, please?** (Mi lahko podaš sol, prosim?) **Could I have the bill, please?** (Lahko prosim račun?) **Of course.** (Seveda.) **Can** je prav med prijatelji.

Kar ti je všeč na splošno: za **like**, **love**, **enjoy** in **hate** pride **-ing**: **I like walking.** **Mrs Birkett enjoys cooking.** Za like, love in hate je prav tudi **to** (**I like to walk**), za enjoy samo -ing (ne *I enjoy to walk*).

**like** je vedno, **'d like** je zdaj: **I like tea.** **I'd like a tea.**
rule.de:
**want to** + Grundform sagt geradeheraus, was du willst: **I want to go home.** (Ich will nach Hause.) **Jack wants to buy a dog.** (Jack will einen Hund kaufen.) Gesprochen hörst du **wanna**.

**would like** (kurz **'d like**) sagt es höflich, für alle gleich. Mit einer Sache: **I'd like a cup of tea.** (Ich hätte gern eine Tasse Tee.) Mit einem Verb **to** + Grundform: **I'd like to stay.** (nicht *I'd like stay*). Anbieten: **Would you like a scone?** (Möchtest du einen Scone?) **Yes, please.** (Ja, bitte.) **No, thank you.** (Nein, danke.) **I'd love to.** (Sehr gern.)

Höflich bitten: **Could you pass the salt, please?** (Könntest du mir bitte das Salz geben?) **Could I have the bill, please?** (Könnte ich bitte die Rechnung haben?) **Of course.** (Natürlich.) **Can** passt unter Freunden.

Was dir allgemein gefällt: Nach **like**, **love**, **enjoy** und **hate** kommt **-ing**: **I like walking.** **Mrs Birkett enjoys cooking.** Nach like, love und hate passt auch **to** (**I like to walk**), nach enjoy nur -ing (nicht *I enjoy to walk*).

**like** ist immer, **'d like** ist jetzt: **I like tea.** **I'd like a tea.**
rule.it:
**want to** + la forma base dice in modo diretto che cosa vuoi: **I want to go home.** (Voglio andare a casa.) **Jack wants to buy a dog.** (Jack vuole comprare un cane.) A voce senti **wanna**.

**would like** (breve **'d like**) lo dice con garbo, uguale per tutti. Con una cosa: **I'd like a cup of tea.** (Vorrei una tazza di tè.) Con un verbo, **to** + la forma base: **I'd like to stay.** (non *I'd like stay*). Per offrire: **Would you like a scone?** (Vuoi uno scone?) **Yes, please.** (Sì, grazie.) **No, thank you.** (No, grazie.) **I'd love to.** (Volentieri.)

Per chiedere con garbo: **Could you pass the salt, please?** (Mi passeresti il sale, per favore?) **Could I have the bill, please?** (Potrei avere il conto, per favore?) **Of course.** (Certo.) **Can** va bene tra amici.

Ciò che ti piace in generale: dopo **like**, **love**, **enjoy** e **hate** viene **-ing**: **I like walking.** **Mrs Birkett enjoys cooking.** Dopo like, love e hate va bene anche **to** (**I like to walk**), dopo enjoy solo -ing (non *I enjoy to walk*).

**like** è sempre, **'d like** è adesso: **I like tea.** **I'd like a tea.**
rule.en:
**want to** + the base form says plainly what you want: **I want to go home.** **Jack wants to buy a dog.** In talk you hear **wanna**.

**would like** (short **'d like**) says it politely, the same for everyone. With a thing: **I'd like a cup of tea.** With a verb, **to** + the base form: **I'd like to stay.** (not *I'd like stay*). To offer: **Would you like a scone?** **Yes, please.** **No, thank you.** **I'd love to.**

To ask politely: **Could you pass the salt, please?** **Could I have the bill, please?** **Of course.** **Can** is right among friends.

What you like in general takes **-ing** after **like**, **love**, **enjoy** and **hate**: **I like walking.** **Mrs Birkett enjoys cooking.** After like, love and hate **to** is right too (**I like to walk**); after enjoy only -ing (not *I enjoy to walk*).

**like** is always, **'d like** is now: **I like tea.** **I'd like a tea.**
